When concentration of ‘X’ is increased to four times, the rate of reaction becomes 16 times. B. The reaction is a second order reaction. C. The half-life period is independent of the concentration of X. D. Decomposition of N $_{2}$ O $_{5}$ is an example of the above reaction. E. vs time is valid for the above reaction. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.question_html:
Consider the reaction aX → bY, for which the rate constant at 30°C is $1 \times 10^{-3}\text{mol}^{-1}\text{L}\text{s}^{-1}$ . Which of the following statements are true?

A. When concentration of ‘X’ is increased to four times, the rate of reaction becomes 16 times.

B. The reaction is a second order reaction.

C. The half-life period is independent of the concentration of X.

D. Decomposition of N $_{2}$ O $_{5}$ is an example of the above reaction.

E. vs time is valid for the above reaction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questions.explanation_text:
The given rate constant is $k=10^{-3}\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ . Step 1: Determining the order of reaction The general unit of the rate constant is $\text{M}^{1-n}\text{s}^{-1}$ , where $n$ is the order of reaction. 

Here, the unit of $k$ is $\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ . So, $1-n=-1 \Rightarrow n=2$ . 

Hence, this is a second order reaction . Step 2: Expression for the rate The rate law for a second order reaction is: $\text{Rate}=k[A]^{2}$ Step 3: Effect of changing concentration If the concentration of $A$ is made 4 times, that is, $[A]^{'}=4[A]$ , then $\text{New rate}=k(4[A])^{2}=16k[A]^{2}$ So, the rate increases by 16 times. 

Therefore, statement (A) is correct. Step 4: Order of reaction As we found $n=2$ , the reaction is second order. 

So, statement (B) is correct. Step 5: Half-life relation For a second order reaction, the half-life is inversely proportional to the initial concentration: $t_{1/2}=\frac{1}{k[A]_{0}}$ Hence, the half-life depends on concentration. 

So, statement (C) is incorrect because it is true only for a first order reaction. Step 6: Example of reaction The decomposition of $N_{2}O_{5}$ is a first order reaction. 

Thus, statement (D) is incorrect. Step 7: Graph type A straight-line graph of $log\frac{[R]_{0}}{[R]_{t}}$ versus $t$ is valid only for first order reactions, not second order. 

Therefore, statement (E) is incorrect. Final Answer: The correct statements are (A) and (B).
questions.explanation_html:
The given rate constant is $k=10^{-3}\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ .

Step 1: Determining the order of reaction

The general unit of the rate constant is $\text{M}^{1-n}\text{s}^{-1}$ , where $n$ is the order of reaction. Here, the unit of $k$ is $\text{M}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ .

So, $1-n=-1 \Rightarrow n=2$ . Hence, this is a second order reaction.

Step 2: Expression for the rate

The rate law for a second order reaction is: $\text{Rate}=k[A]^{2}$

Step 3: Effect of changing concentration

If the concentration of $A$ is made 4 times, that is, $[A]^{'}=4[A]$ , then $\text{New rate}=k(4[A])^{2}=16k[A]^{2}$ So, the rate increases by 16 times. Therefore, statement (A) is correct.

Step 4: Order of reaction

As we found $n=2$ , the reaction is second order. So, statement (B) is correct.

Step 5: Half-life relation

For a second order reaction, the half-life is inversely proportional to the initial concentration: $t_{1/2}=\frac{1}{k[A]_{0}}$ Hence, the half-life depends on concentration. So, statement (C) is incorrect because it is true only for a first order reaction.

Step 6: Example of reaction

The decomposition of $N_{2}O_{5}$ is a first order reaction. Thus, statement (D) is incorrect.

Step 7: Graph type

A straight-line graph of $log\frac{[R]_{0}}{[R]_{t}}$ versus $t$ is valid only for first order reactions, not second order. Therefore, statement (E) is incorrect.

Final Answer: The correct statements are (A) and (B).

questions.question_text: At $27^{\circ}C$ in presence of a catalyst, activation energy of a reaction is lowered by $10kJmol^{-1}$ . The logarithm of ratio of $\frac{k\text{(catalysed)}}{k\text{(uncatalysed)}}$ is…. (Consider that the frequency factor for both the reactions is same)
questions.question_html:
At $27^{\circ}C$ in presence of a catalyst, activation energy of a reaction is lowered by $10kJmol^{-1}$ . The logarithm of ratio of $\frac{k\text{(catalysed)}}{k\text{(uncatalysed)}}$ is….

(Consider that the frequency factor for both the reactions is same)
questions.explanation_text: Arrhenius equation (NCERT): $k=Ae^{-\frac{E_{a}}{RT}}$ Given: catalyst lowers activation energy by $10\text{kJ mol}^{-1}=10000\text{J mol}^{-1}$ and frequency factor $A$ is same. So, $\frac{k_{\text{cat}}}{k_{\text{uncat}}}=\frac{Ae^{-\frac{E_{a,\text{cat}}}{RT}}}{Ae^{-\frac{E_{a,\text{uncat}}}{RT}}}=e^{\frac{E_{a,\text{uncat}}-E_{a,\text{cat}}}{RT}}=e^{\frac{10000}{RT}}$ At $27^{\circ}\text{C}$ , $T=300\text{K}$ and $R=8.314\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ : $\frac{10000}{RT}=\frac{10000}{8.314 \times 300} \approx 4.009$ So, $log_{10}(\frac{k_{\text{cat}}}{k_{\text{uncat}}})=log_{10}(e^{4.009})=\frac{4.009}{2.303} \approx 1.741$ Correct option: A (1.741)
questions.explanation_html:
Arrhenius equation (NCERT):

$k=Ae^{-\frac{E_{a}}{RT}}$

Given: catalyst lowers activation energy by $10\text{kJ mol}^{-1}=10000\text{J mol}^{-1}$ and frequency factor $A$ is same.

So,

$\frac{k_{\text{cat}}}{k_{\text{uncat}}}=\frac{Ae^{-\frac{E_{a,\text{cat}}}{RT}}}{Ae^{-\frac{E_{a,\text{uncat}}}{RT}}}=e^{\frac{E_{a,\text{uncat}}-E_{a,\text{cat}}}{RT}}=e^{\frac{10000}{RT}}$

At $27^{\circ}\text{C}$ , $T=300\text{K}$ and $R=8.314\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ :

$\frac{10000}{RT}=\frac{10000}{8.314 \times 300} \approx 4.009$

So,

$log_{10}(\frac{k_{\text{cat}}}{k_{\text{uncat}}})=log_{10}(e^{4.009})=\frac{4.009}{2.303} \approx 1.741$

Correct option: A (1.741)

Three sets of experiment were performed for a reaction under similar experimental conditions:

Run $1 \Rightarrow 100mL$ of 10 M solution of reactant A

Run $2 \Rightarrow 200mL$ of 10 M solution of reactant A

Run $3 \Rightarrow 100mL$ of 10 M solution of reactant $A+100mL$ of $H_{2}O$ added.

The correct variation of rate of reaction is

questions.explanation_text: For a first order reaction, the rate law is: Rate $=k[A]$ This means the rate depends only on the concentration of $A$ , not on the total volume taken. Run 1: $100mL$ of $10M$ $A$ is used, so $[A]=10M$ . Run 2: $200mL$ of $10M$ $A$ is used, but the concentration is still $[A]=10M$ (only volume increased, not concentration). Run 3: $100mL$ of $10M$ $A$ is mixed with $100mL$ of water, so the solution gets diluted to double the volume. So the new concentration becomes: $[A]=\frac{10 \times 100}{100+100}=5M$ Since Rate $=k[A]$ , the rates are: Run 1: Rate $=k(10)$ Run 2: Rate $=k(10)$ Run 3: Rate $=k(5)$ So, the correct variation is: $\text{Rate}_{1}=\text{Rate}_{2}>\text{Rate}_{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
For a first order reaction, the rate law is:

Rate $=k[A]$

This means the rate depends only on the concentration of $A$ , not on the total volume taken.

Run 1: $100mL$ of $10M$ $A$ is used, so $[A]=10M$ .

Run 2: $200mL$ of $10M$ $A$ is used, but the concentration is still $[A]=10M$ (only volume increased, not concentration).

Run 3: $100mL$ of $10M$ $A$ is mixed with $100mL$ of water, so the solution gets diluted to double the volume.

So the new concentration becomes:

$[A]=\frac{10 \times 100}{100+100}=5M$

Since Rate $=k[A]$ , the rates are:

Run 1: Rate $=k(10)$

Run 2: Rate $=k(10)$

Run 3: Rate $=k(5)$

So, the correct variation is:

$\text{Rate}_{1}=\text{Rate}_{2}>\text{Rate}_{3}$

questions.question_text: If the half life of a first order reaction is 6.93 minutes then the time required for completion of $99%$ of the reaction will be $____$ minutes. (Given $:log2=0.3010$ )
questions.question_html:
If the half life of a first order reaction is 6.93 minutes then the time required for completion of $99%$ of the reaction will be $____$ minutes.

(Given $:log2=0.3010$ )
questions.explanation_text: For a first order reaction, $t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$ Given: $t_{1/2}=6.93\text{min}$ So, $k=\frac{0.693}{6.93}=0.1\text{min}^{-1}$ Now, $99%$ completion means only $1%$ of the reactant is left. So, $\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]}=\frac{100}{1}=100$ For a first order reaction, $t=\frac{2.303}{k}log\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]}$ Substituting the values: $t=\frac{2.303}{0.1}log100$ Since, $log100=2$ therefore, $t=\frac{2.303}{0.1} \times 2$ $t=23.03 \times 2=46.06\text{min}$ Hence, the time required for $99%$ completion of the reaction is $46.06\text{minutes}$
questions.explanation_html:
For a first order reaction,

$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$

Given:

$t_{1/2}=6.93\text{min}$

So,

$k=\frac{0.693}{6.93}=0.1\text{min}^{-1}$

Now, $99%$ completion means only $1%$ of the reactant is left.

So,

$\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]}=\frac{100}{1}=100$

For a first order reaction,

$t=\frac{2.303}{k}log\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]}$

Substituting the values:

$t=\frac{2.303}{0.1}log100$

Since,

$log100=2$

therefore,

$t=\frac{2.303}{0.1} \times 2$

$t=23.03 \times 2=46.06\text{min}$

Hence, the time required for $99%$ completion of the reaction is

$46.06\text{minutes}$

First order gas phase reaction

$A \rightarrow B+C$

$p_{t}=$ initial pressure of gas $A,p_{t}=$ total pressure of the reaction mixture at time $t$

Expression of rate constant ( $k$ ) is
questions.explanation_text: So, total pressure at time $t$ is $p_{t}=(p_{i}-x)+x+x=p_{i}+x$ Hence, $x=p_{t}-p_{i}$ Now pressure of $A$ at time $t$ is $p_{A}=p_{i}-x$ Substituting $x=p_{t}-p_{i}$ : $p_{A}=p_{i}-(p_{t}-p_{i})=2p_{i}-p_{t}$ For a first-order reaction, $k=\frac{1}{t}ln\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{t}}$ Since pressure is proportional to concentration for gases, $k=\frac{1}{t}ln\frac{p_{i}}{2p_{i}-p_{t}}$ Therefore, the correct expression is $k=\frac{1}{t}ln\frac{p_{i}}{2p_{i}-p_{t}}$ So, the correct option is: $\text{Option A}$
questions.explanation_html:
So, total pressure at time $t$ is

$p_{t}=(p_{i}-x)+x+x=p_{i}+x$

Hence,

$x=p_{t}-p_{i}$

Now pressure of $A$ at time $t$ is

$p_{A}=p_{i}-x$

Substituting $x=p_{t}-p_{i}$ :

$p_{A}=p_{i}-(p_{t}-p_{i})=2p_{i}-p_{t}$

For a first-order reaction,

$k=\frac{1}{t}ln\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{t}}$

Since pressure is proportional to concentration for gases,

$k=\frac{1}{t}ln\frac{p_{i}}{2p_{i}-p_{t}}$

Therefore, the correct expression is

$k=\frac{1}{t}ln\frac{p_{i}}{2p_{i}-p_{t}}$

So, the correct option is:

$\text{Option A}$

questions.question_text: t 100% is the time required for the 100% completion of the reaction while t 1/2 is the time required for 50% of the reaction to be completed. Which of the following option correctly represents the relation between t 100% and t 1/2 for zero and first order reactions respectively?
questions.question_html: t100% is the time required for the 100% completion of the reaction while t1/2 is the time required for 50% of the reaction to be completed. Which of the following option correctly represents the relation between t100% and t1/2 for zero and first order reactions respectively?
questions.explanation_text: For a zero order reaction : The integrated rate law is $[A]_{t}=[A]_{0}-kt$ For 100% completion , $[A]_{t}=0$ . So, $0=[A]_{0}-kt_{100%}$ $t_{100%}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{k}$ For half-life , $[A]_{t}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{2}$ . So, $\frac{[A]_{0}}{2}=[A]_{0}-kt_{1/2}$ $kt_{1/2}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{2}$ $t_{1/2}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{2k}$ Hence, $t_{100%}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{k}=2(\frac{[A]_{0}}{2k})=2t_{1/2}$ So for zero order , $t_{100%}=2t_{1/2}$ For a first order reaction : The integrated rate law is $[A]_{t}=[A]_{0}e^{-kt}$ For 100% completion , we need $[A]_{t}=0$ . That means $0=[A]_{0}e^{-kt}$ But $e^{-kt}$ can never become exactly zero for any finite value of $t$ . So, the reaction takes infinite time for complete consumption. Thus, $t_{100%}=\infty$ Also, for first order reaction, $t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$ Hence $t_{100%}$ is not a finite multiple of $t_{1/2}$ , rather it is effectively represented as infinite. So the correct relation is: Zero order: $t_{100%}=2t_{1/2}$ First order: $t_{100%}=(t_{1/2})^{\infty}$ in the given options, meaning complete reaction requires infinite time. Therefore, the correct option is: $\text{Option B}$
questions.explanation_html:
For a zero order reaction:

The integrated rate law is

$[A]_{t}=[A]_{0}-kt$

For 100% completion, $[A]_{t}=0$ .

So,

$0=[A]_{0}-kt_{100%}$

$t_{100%}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{k}$

For half-life, $[A]_{t}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{2}$ .

So,

$\frac{[A]_{0}}{2}=[A]_{0}-kt_{1/2}$

$kt_{1/2}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{2}$

$t_{1/2}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{2k}$

Hence,

$t_{100%}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{k}=2(\frac{[A]_{0}}{2k})=2t_{1/2}$

So for zero order,

$t_{100%}=2t_{1/2}$

For a first order reaction:

The integrated rate law is

$[A]_{t}=[A]_{0}e^{-kt}$

For 100% completion, we need $[A]_{t}=0$ .

That means

$0=[A]_{0}e^{-kt}$

But $e^{-kt}$ can never become exactly zero for any finite value of $t$ .

So, the reaction takes infinite time for complete consumption.

Thus,

$t_{100%}=\infty$

Also, for first order reaction,

$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$

Hence $t_{100%}$ is not a finite multiple of $t_{1/2}$ , rather it is effectively represented as infinite.

So the correct relation is:

  • Zero order: $t_{100%}=2t_{1/2}$

  • First order: $t_{100%}=(t_{1/2})^{\infty}$ in the given options, meaning complete reaction requires infinite time.

Therefore, the correct option is:

$\text{Option B}$

questions.explanation_text: From the graph, in the first $10$ minutes the concentration of $A$ decreases from $0.05$ to $0.04$ . So, amount of $A$ dissociated in $10$ minutes $=0.05-0.04=0.01$ . For the reaction $A \rightarrow nB$ , when $0.01$ of $A$ reacts, $B$ formed $=0.01 \times n$ . From the graph, in the same time interval, concentration of $B$ formed becomes $0.03$ . So we equate $0.01 \times n$ to $0.03$ and find $n$ . $\begin{aligned} & A \rightarrow nB \\ & 0.050 \\ & 0.040.01 \times n \\ & 0.01 \times n=0.03 \\ & n=3 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
From the graph, in the first $10$ minutes the concentration of $A$ decreases from $0.05$ to $0.04$ .

So, amount of $A$ dissociated in $10$ minutes $=0.05-0.04=0.01$ .

For the reaction $A \rightarrow nB$ , when $0.01$ of $A$ reacts, $B$ formed $=0.01 \times n$ .

From the graph, in the same time interval, concentration of $B$ formed becomes $0.03$ . So we equate $0.01 \times n$ to $0.03$ and find $n$ .

$\begin{aligned} & A \rightarrow nB \\ & 0.050 \\ & 0.040.01 \times n \\ & 0.01 \times n=0.03 \\ & n=3 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Let initial pressure of $A$ be $P_{0}=1$ bar in a $1\text{L}$ closed vessel at constant $T$ . For the reaction: $A(g) \rightarrow B(g)+C(g)$ Suppose $x$ bar (in pressure-equivalent terms) of $A$ decomposes. Then after time $t$ : Pressure of $A$ left $=(1-x)$ bar Pressure of $B$ formed $=x$ bar Pressure of $C$ formed $=x$ bar So total pressure: $P_{\text{total}}=(1-x)+x+x=1+x$ Given after $100$ min, $P_{\text{total}}=1.5$ bar: $1+x=1.5 \Rightarrow x=0.5$ So partial pressure of $A$ after $100$ min: $P_{A}=1-x=1-0.5=0.5\text{bar}$ For a first order reaction: $k=\frac{2.303}{t}log(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{t}})$ Here, pressure is proportional to concentration, so: $k=\frac{2.303}{100}log(\frac{1}{0.5})$ $=\frac{2.303}{100}log2$ Given $log2=0.3$ : $k=\frac{2.303}{100} \times 0.3=6.9 \times 10^{-3}\text{min}^{-1}$ Correct option: B) $6.9 \times 10^{-3}\text{min}^{-1}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let initial pressure of $A$ be $P_{0}=1$ bar in a $1\text{L}$ closed vessel at constant $T$ .

For the reaction:

$A(g) \rightarrow B(g)+C(g)$

Suppose $x$ bar (in pressure-equivalent terms) of $A$ decomposes.

Then after time $t$ :

  • Pressure of $A$ left $=(1-x)$ bar

  • Pressure of $B$ formed $=x$ bar

  • Pressure of $C$ formed $=x$ bar

So total pressure:

$P_{\text{total}}=(1-x)+x+x=1+x$

Given after $100$ min, $P_{\text{total}}=1.5$ bar:

$1+x=1.5 \Rightarrow x=0.5$

So partial pressure of $A$ after $100$ min:

$P_{A}=1-x=1-0.5=0.5\text{bar}$

For a first order reaction:

$k=\frac{2.303}{t}log(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{t}})$

Here, pressure is proportional to concentration, so:

$k=\frac{2.303}{100}log(\frac{1}{0.5})$

$=\frac{2.303}{100}log2$

Given $log2=0.3$ :

$k=\frac{2.303}{100} \times 0.3=6.9 \times 10^{-3}\text{min}^{-1}$

Correct option: B) $6.9 \times 10^{-3}\text{min}^{-1}$

questions.explanation_text: For a first order reaction, the integrated rate law is $k=\frac{2.303}{t}log\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{t}}$ We use the data at $t=20$ min: Initial concentration, $[A]_{0}=0.6500\text{M}$ Concentration at $20$ min, $[A]_{20}=0.00065\text{M}$ So, $k=\frac{2.303}{20}log\frac{0.6500}{0.00065}$ Now, $\frac{0.6500}{0.00065}=1000$ and $log1000=3$ Therefore, $k=\frac{2.303}{20} \times 3$ $k=\frac{6.909}{20}$ $k=0.34545\text{min}^{-1}$ Now we use the concentration at time $x$ : $[A]_{x}=0.0650\text{M}$ Again, $k=\frac{2.303}{x}log\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{x}}$ $0.34545=\frac{2.303}{x}log\frac{0.6500}{0.0650}$ Now, $\frac{0.6500}{0.0650}=10$ and $log10=1$ So, $0.34545=\frac{2.303}{x}$ Hence, $x=\frac{2.303}{0.34545}$ $x \approx 6.67\text{min}$ Nearest integer: $7\text{min}$

For a first order reaction, the integrated rate law is

We use the data at $t=20$ min:

So,

$k=\frac{2.303}{20}log\frac{0.6500}{0.00065}$

Now,

$\frac{0.6500}{0.00065}=1000$

and

Therefore,

$k=\frac{2.303}{20} \times 3$

$k=\frac{6.909}{20}$

Again,

$0.34545=\frac{2.303}{x}log\frac{0.6500}{0.0650}$

Now,

$\frac{0.6500}{0.0650}=10$

questions.question_text: The half-life of $^{65}Zn$ is 245 days. After $x$ days, $75%$ of original activity remained. The value of $x$ in days is $____$ . (Nearest integer) (Given: $log3=0.4771$ and $log2=0.3010$ )
questions.question_html:
The half-life of $^{65}Zn$ is 245 days. After $x$ days, $75%$ of original activity remained. The value of $x$ in days is $____$ . (Nearest integer)

(Given: $log3=0.4771$ and $log2=0.3010$ )
questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} & t_{1/2}=\frac{ln2}{K} \end{aligned}$ Here, $t_{1/2}=245$ days, so we find $K$ as: $\begin{aligned} & K=\frac{ln2}{245} \end{aligned}$ Now we use the radioactive decay relation for activity: $\begin{aligned} & t=\frac{1}{K}ln\frac{a_{0}}{a_{t}} \end{aligned}$ Given that $75%$ of the original activity remains, so $a_{t}=0.75a_{0}=\frac{3}{4}a_{0}$ . So, $\begin{aligned} & \frac{a_{0}}{a_{t}}=\frac{a_{0}}{\frac{3}{4}a_{0}}=\frac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$ Therefore, $\begin{aligned} & t_{25%}=\frac{1}{K}ln\frac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$ Substitute $K=\frac{ln2}{245}$ : $\begin{aligned} & t_{25%}=\frac{1}{\frac{ln2}{245}}ln\frac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$ Simplifying: $\begin{aligned} & t_{25%}=245\frac{ln\frac{4}{3}}{\ell n2}=245[\frac{2log2-log3}{log2}] \end{aligned}$ Now use the given values $log3=0.4771$ and $log2=0.3010$ : $\begin{aligned} & =245[\frac{2 \times 0.3010-0.4771}{0.3010}]=101.66\text{day.} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & t_{1/2}=\frac{ln2}{K} \end{aligned}$

Here, $t_{1/2}=245$ days, so we find $K$ as:

$\begin{aligned} & K=\frac{ln2}{245} \end{aligned}$

Now we use the radioactive decay relation for activity:

$\begin{aligned} & t=\frac{1}{K}ln\frac{a_{0}}{a_{t}} \end{aligned}$

Given that $75%$ of the original activity remains, so $a_{t}=0.75a_{0}=\frac{3}{4}a_{0}$ .

So,

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{a_{0}}{a_{t}}=\frac{a_{0}}{\frac{3}{4}a_{0}}=\frac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$

Therefore,

$\begin{aligned} & t_{25%}=\frac{1}{K}ln\frac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$

Substitute $K=\frac{ln2}{245}$ :

$\begin{aligned} & t_{25%}=\frac{1}{\frac{ln2}{245}}ln\frac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$

Simplifying:

Now use the given values $log3=0.4771$ and $log2=0.3010$ :

questions.question_text: Pre-exponential factors of two different reactions of same order are identical. Let activation energy of first reaction exceeds the activation energy of second reaction by $20kJmol^{-1}$ . If $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ are the rate constants of first and second reaction respectively at 300 K , then $ln\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}$ will be $____$ . (nearest integer) $[R=8.3JK^{-1}mol^{-1}]$
questions.question_html: Pre-exponential factors of two different reactions of same order are identical. Let activation energy of first reaction exceeds the activation energy of second reaction by $20kJmol^{-1}$ . If $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ are the rate constants of first and second reaction respectively at 300 K , then $ln\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}$ will be $____$ . (nearest integer) $[R=8.3JK^{-1}mol^{-1}]$
questions.explanation_text: Arrhenius equation: $k=Ae^{-E_{a}/RT}$ Given pre-exponential factors are identical, so $A_{1}=A_{2}$ . Also, activation energy of first reaction exceeds that of second by $20\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ : $E_{a1}=E_{a2}+20,000\text{J mol}^{-1}$ Now, $\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}=\frac{Ae^{-E_{a2}/RT}}{Ae^{-E_{a1}/RT}}=e^{-(E_{a2}-E_{a1})/RT}=e^{(E_{a1}-E_{a2})/RT}$ So, $ln(\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}})=\frac{E_{a1}-E_{a2}}{RT}=\frac{20,000}{8.3 \times 300}$ Compute: $8.3 \times 300=2490$ $ln(\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}})=\frac{20,000}{2490} \approx 8.03$ Nearest integer: $8$
questions.explanation_html:
Arrhenius equation:

$k=Ae^{-E_{a}/RT}$

Given pre-exponential factors are identical, so $A_{1}=A_{2}$ .

Also, activation energy of first reaction exceeds that of second by $20\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ :

$E_{a1}=E_{a2}+20,000\text{J mol}^{-1}$

Now,

$\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}=\frac{Ae^{-E_{a2}/RT}}{Ae^{-E_{a1}/RT}}=e^{-(E_{a2}-E_{a1})/RT}=e^{(E_{a1}-E_{a2})/RT}$

So,

$ln(\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}})=\frac{E_{a1}-E_{a2}}{RT}=\frac{20,000}{8.3 \times 300}$

Compute:

$8.3 \times 300=2490$

$ln(\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}})=\frac{20,000}{2490} \approx 8.03$

Nearest integer:

$8$

questions.question_text: Consider the given graph showing variation of reactant concentration with time. Three different reactions were started with identical initial concentration of reactants. Which of the following statement is correct?
questions.question_html:
Consider the given graph showing variation of reactant concentration with time.

Three different reactions were started with identical initial concentration of reactants. Which of the following statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The order of all the three reactions is same.
options.html: The order of all the three reactions is same.

options.label: B
options.text: The rate constant of reaction 3 is larger than the rate constant of reaction 2 if the order of reaction is same for both.
options.html: The rate constant of reaction 3 is larger than the rate constant of reaction 2 if the order of reaction is same for both.

options.label: C
options.text: The SI unit of rate constant of reaction 1 is $s^{-1}$ .
options.html: The SI unit of rate constant of reaction 1 is $s^{-1}$ .

options.label: D
options.text: Thermal decomposition of HI on gold surface is an example of reaction 2 .
options.html: Thermal decomposition of HI on gold surface is an example of reaction 2 .

questions.explanation_text: (A) The order of the reactions cannot be the same because curve (1) is a straight line, but curves (2) and (3) decrease exponentially with time. A straight-line decrease of reactant concentration with time is the characteristic of a zero order reaction. Exponentially decaying curves are usually seen in first order (and sometimes other) reactions. Rate expression for $n=0$ : $\begin{aligned} & Kt=[A_{0}]-[A]=[R_{0}]-[R] \\ & [R]=[R_{0}]-kt( \because y=c+mx) \\ & \text{slope}(m)=-k \end{aligned}$ So, graph (1) matches the straight-line form $[R]=[R_{0}]-kt$ , hence reaction (1) is zero order. (B) Now assume that reactions (2) and (3) are first order reactions (their curves look exponential). $\begin{aligned} [R] & =[R_{0}]e^{-kt} \\ \text{At}t & =\text{constant} \\ [R_{3}] & <[R_{2}] \end{aligned}$ At the same time $t$ , curve (3) shows a smaller concentration than curve (2), i.e. $[R_{3}]<[R_{2}]$ . This means reaction (3) is consuming reactant faster, so it has a larger rate constant. And since Rate of reaction: $\begin{aligned} R=K[A]\text{or}K[R] \\ K∝\frac{1}{[R]} \end{aligned}$ Hence, $K_{3}>K_{2}$ . (c) SI unit for rate constant $(k)=mol^{1-n}L^{n-1}s^{-1}$ . For 1st reaction order $(n)=0$ . Then si unit $=mol^{1-0}L^{0-1}s^{-1}$ $=molL^{-1}s^{-1}.$ (D) Thermal decomposition of HI on Gold is an example of zero-order reaction because its rate expression is written as: $R=K[HI]^{0}$
questions.explanation_html:
(A) The order of the reactions cannot be the same because curve (1) is a straight line, but curves (2) and (3) decrease exponentially with time.

A straight-line decrease of reactant concentration with time is the characteristic of a zero order reaction. Exponentially decaying curves are usually seen in first order (and sometimes other) reactions.

Rate expression for $n=0$ :

$\begin{aligned} & Kt=[A_{0}]-[A]=[R_{0}]-[R] \\ & [R]=[R_{0}]-kt( \because y=c+mx) \\ & \text{slope}(m)=-k \end{aligned}$

So, graph (1) matches the straight-line form $[R]=[R_{0}]-kt$ , hence reaction (1) is zero order.

(B) Now assume that reactions (2) and (3) are first order reactions (their curves look exponential).

$\begin{aligned} [R] & =[R_{0}]e^{-kt} \\ \text{At}t & =\text{constant} \\ [R_{3}] & <[R_{2}] \end{aligned}$

At the same time $t$ , curve (3) shows a smaller concentration than curve (2), i.e. $[R_{3}]<[R_{2}]$ . This means reaction (3) is consuming reactant faster, so it has a larger rate constant.

And since Rate of reaction:

$\begin{aligned} R=K[A]\text{or}K[R] \\ K∝\frac{1}{[R]} \end{aligned}$

Hence, $K_{3}>K_{2}$ .

(c) SI unit for rate constant $(k)=mol^{1-n}L^{n-1}s^{-1}$ . For 1st reaction order $(n)=0$ .

Then si unit $=mol^{1-0}L^{0-1}s^{-1}$

$=molL^{-1}s^{-1}.$

(D) Thermal decomposition of HI on Gold is an example of zero-order reaction because its rate expression is written as:

$R=K[HI]^{0}$

questions.question_text: An organic compound undergoes first order decomposition. The time taken for decomposition to $(\frac{1}{8})^{\text{th}}$ and $(\frac{1}{10})^{\text{th}}$ of its initial concentration are $t_{1/8}$ and $t_{1/10}$ respectively. What is the value of $\frac{t_{1/8}}{t_{1/10}} \times 10$ ? $(log2=0.3)$
questions.question_html:
An organic compound undergoes first order decomposition. The time taken for decomposition to $(\frac{1}{8})^{\text{th}}$ and $(\frac{1}{10})^{\text{th}}$ of its initial concentration are $t_{1/8}$ and $t_{1/10}$ respectively.

What is the value of $\frac{t_{1/8}}{t_{1/10}} \times 10$ ?

$(log2=0.3)$
questions.explanation_text: For a first order reaction, the integrated rate law is $t=\frac{2.303}{k}log(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{t}})$ 1) Time to reach $(\frac{1}{8})^{\text{th}}$ of initial concentration Here, $[A]_{t}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{8}$ $t_{1/8}=\frac{2.303}{k}log(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{0}/8})=\frac{2.303}{k}log(8)$ Now, $log(8)=log(2^{3})=3log2=3 \times 0.3=0.9$ So, $t_{1/8}=\frac{2.303}{k} \times 0.9$ 2) Time to reach $(\frac{1}{10})^{\text{th}}$ of initial concentration Here, $[A]_{t}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{10}$ $t_{1/10}=\frac{2.303}{k}log(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{0}/10})=\frac{2.303}{k}log(10)$ And $log(10)=1$ , so $t_{1/10}=\frac{2.303}{k} \times 1$ 3) Required ratio $\frac{t_{1/8}}{t_{1/10}}=\frac{\frac{2.303}{k} \times 0.9}{\frac{2.303}{k} \times 1}=0.9$ So, $\frac{t_{1/8}}{t_{1/10}} \times 10=0.9 \times 10=9$ Correct option: B (9)
questions.explanation_html:
For a first order reaction, the integrated rate law is

$t=\frac{2.303}{k}log(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{t}})$

1) Time to reach $(\frac{1}{8})^{\text{th}}$ of initial concentration

Here, $[A]_{t}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{8}$

$t_{1/8}=\frac{2.303}{k}log(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{0}/8})=\frac{2.303}{k}log(8)$

Now, $log(8)=log(2^{3})=3log2=3 \times 0.3=0.9$

So,

$t_{1/8}=\frac{2.303}{k} \times 0.9$

2) Time to reach $(\frac{1}{10})^{\text{th}}$ of initial concentration

Here, $[A]_{t}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{10}$

$t_{1/10}=\frac{2.303}{k}log(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{0}/10})=\frac{2.303}{k}log(10)$

And $log(10)=1$ , so

$t_{1/10}=\frac{2.303}{k} \times 1$

3) Required ratio

$\frac{t_{1/8}}{t_{1/10}}=\frac{\frac{2.303}{k} \times 0.9}{\frac{2.303}{k} \times 1}=0.9$

So,

$\frac{t_{1/8}}{t_{1/10}} \times 10=0.9 \times 10=9$

Correct option: B (9)

questions.question_text: Observe the following reactions at $T(K)$ . I. $A \rightarrow$ products. II. $5Br^{-}(aq)+BrO_{3}^{-}(aq)+6H^{+}(aq) \rightarrow 3Br_{2}(aq)+3H_{2}O(l)$ Both the reactions are started at 10.00 am . The rates of these reactions at 10.10 am are same. The value of $-\frac{\Delta[Br^{-}]}{\Delta t}$ at 10.10 am is $2 \times 10^{-4}molL^{-1}min^{-1}$ . The concentration of A at 10.10 am is $10^{-2}molL^{-1}$ . What is the first order rate constant (in $min^{-1}$ ) of reaction $I$ ?
questions.question_html:
Observe the following reactions at $T(K)$ .

I. $A \rightarrow$ products.

II. $5Br^{-}(aq)+BrO_{3}^{-}(aq)+6H^{+}(aq) \rightarrow 3Br_{2}(aq)+3H_{2}O(l)$

Both the reactions are started at 10.00 am . The rates of these reactions at 10.10 am are same. The value of $-\frac{\Delta[Br^{-}]}{\Delta t}$ at 10.10 am is $2 \times 10^{-4}molL^{-1}min^{-1}$ . The concentration of A at 10.10 am is $10^{-2}molL^{-1}$ . What is the first order rate constant (in $min^{-1}$ ) of reaction $I$ ?
questions.explanation_text: At $t=10$ minutes (i.e., at 10:10 am) For reaction II, $5Br^{-}$ are consumed when the reaction proceeds once. So, the rate of reaction is related to the rate of decrease of $[Br^{-}]$ as: $\begin{aligned} & \text{Rate of reaction}=-\frac{1}{5}\frac{\Delta[Br^{-}]}{\Delta t}=\frac{1}{5} \times (2 \times 10^{-4}) \\ & =4 \times 10^{-5} \end{aligned}$ Now consider reaction I: $A \rightarrow$ products. At $t=10$ minutes, both reactions have the same rate. So, the rate of reaction I at this time is also $4 \times 10^{-5}molL^{-1}min^{-1}$ . Since reaction I is first order, its rate law is: Rate of reaction $=k[A]$ Given $[A]=10^{-2}molL^{-1}$ at 10:10 am, we write: Rate of reaction $=4 \times 10^{-5}=k[A]$ So, $k=\frac{4 \times 10^{-5}}{10^{-2}}=4 \times 10^{-3}min^{-1}.$
questions.explanation_html:
At $t=10$ minutes (i.e., at 10:10 am)

For reaction II, $5Br^{-}$ are consumed when the reaction proceeds once. So, the rate of reaction is related to the rate of decrease of $[Br^{-}]$ as:

$\begin{aligned} & \text{Rate of reaction}=-\frac{1}{5}\frac{\Delta[Br^{-}]}{\Delta t}=\frac{1}{5} \times (2 \times 10^{-4}) \\ & =4 \times 10^{-5} \end{aligned}$

Now consider reaction I: $A \rightarrow$ products.

At $t=10$ minutes, both reactions have the same rate. So, the rate of reaction I at this time is also $4 \times 10^{-5}molL^{-1}min^{-1}$ .

Since reaction I is first order, its rate law is:

Rate of reaction $=k[A]$

Given $[A]=10^{-2}molL^{-1}$ at 10:10 am, we write:

Rate of reaction $=4 \times 10^{-5}=k[A]$

So,

$k=\frac{4 \times 10^{-5}}{10^{-2}}=4 \times 10^{-3}min^{-1}.$

questions.question_text: Consider the following gas phase reaction being carried out in a closed vessel at $25^{\circ}$ C. $2A(g) \longrightarrow 4B(g)+C(g)$ time (min) total pressure of the system (mm Hg) 30 300 ∞ 600 The pressure of C(g) at 30 minutes time interval would be ________ mm Hg. (nearest integer)
questions.question_html:
Consider the following gas phase reaction being carried out in a closed vessel at $25^{\circ}$ C.

$2A(g) \longrightarrow 4B(g)+C(g)$

time
(min)		total pressure of the
system
(mm Hg)
30300
∞600

The pressure of C(g) at 30 minutes time interval would be ________ mm Hg. (nearest integer)
questions.explanation_text: For the reaction $2A(g) \longrightarrow 4B(g)+C(g)$ let the initial pressure of $A$ be $P_{0}$ . Since the vessel is closed and temperature is constant, pressure is proportional to number of moles. At $t=\infty$ , reaction is complete. From the stoichiometry: $2$ moles of $A$ produce $4+1=5$ moles of products So if initially only $A$ is present, total moles increase by a factor $\frac{5}{2}$ Hence final total pressure is $P_{\infty}=\frac{5}{2}P_{0}$ Given: $P_{\infty}=600\text{mm Hg}$ So, $\frac{5}{2}P_{0}=600$ $P_{0}=600 \times \frac{2}{5}=240\text{mm Hg}$ Now at $30$ min, let the extent of reaction correspond to consumption of $x$ pressure units of $A$ according to: $2A \rightarrow 4B+C$ Then pressure changes are: $A$ : decreases by $x$ $B$ : increases by $2x$ $C$ : increases by $\frac{x}{2}$ This is because for $2A \rightarrow 4B+C$ , if $2$ units of $A$ react, $4$ units of $B$ and $1$ unit of $C$ are formed. So total pressure at time $t$ is $P_{t}=(240-x)+2x+\frac{x}{2}$ $P_{t}=240+\frac{3x}{2}$ Given at $30$ min, $240+\frac{3x}{2}=300$ $\frac{3x}{2}=60$ $x=40$ Therefore pressure of $C$ at $30$ min is $P_{C}=\frac{x}{2}=20\text{mm Hg}$ So, the required pressure is $20\text{mm Hg}$
questions.explanation_html:
For the reaction

$2A(g) \longrightarrow 4B(g)+C(g)$

let the initial pressure of $A$ be $P_{0}$ .

Since the vessel is closed and temperature is constant, pressure is proportional to number of moles.

At $t=\infty$ , reaction is complete.

From the stoichiometry:

  • $2$ moles of $A$ produce $4+1=5$ moles of products

So if initially only $A$ is present, total moles increase by a factor

$\frac{5}{2}$

Hence final total pressure is

$P_{\infty}=\frac{5}{2}P_{0}$

Given:

$P_{\infty}=600\text{mm Hg}$

So,

$\frac{5}{2}P_{0}=600$

$P_{0}=600 \times \frac{2}{5}=240\text{mm Hg}$

Now at $30$ min, let the extent of reaction correspond to consumption of $x$ pressure units of $A$ according to:

$2A \rightarrow 4B+C$

Then pressure changes are:

  • $A$ : decreases by $x$

  • $B$ : increases by $2x$

  • $C$ : increases by $\frac{x}{2}$

This is because for $2A \rightarrow 4B+C$ ,

if $2$ units of $A$ react, $4$ units of $B$ and $1$ unit of $C$ are formed.

So total pressure at time $t$ is

$P_{t}=(240-x)+2x+\frac{x}{2}$

$P_{t}=240+\frac{3x}{2}$

Given at $30$ min,

$240+\frac{3x}{2}=300$

$\frac{3x}{2}=60$

$x=40$

Therefore pressure of $C$ at $30$ min is

$P_{C}=\frac{x}{2}=20\text{mm Hg}$

So, the required pressure is

questions.question_text: For the thermal decomposition of reactant $AB(g)$ , the following plot is constructed. The half life of the reaction is ' $x^{'}min$ . $x=$ $____$ min. (Nearest integer)
questions.question_html:
For the thermal decomposition of reactant $AB(g)$ , the following plot is constructed.

The half life of the reaction is ' $x^{'}min$ .

$x=$ $____$ min. (Nearest integer)
questions.explanation_text: The graph between concentration $[AB]$ and time $t$ is a straight line that decreases with time. This type of graph shows that the reaction is zero order in $[AB]$ . For a zero-order reaction, the integrated rate law is: $\begin{aligned} & [AB]_{0}-[AB]_{t}=kt \\ & 𝟎.𝟔𝟎-𝟎.𝟓𝟓=k(100) \\ & k=5 \times 10^{-4} \\ & \text{Half life}(t_{1/2})=\frac{[AB]_{0}}{2k} \\ & =\frac{0.60}{2 \times 5 \times 10^{-4}} \\ & =600sec \\ & =10min \end{aligned}$ From the graph, the initial concentration is $[AB]_{0}=0.60$ and after $100\text{s}$ the concentration is $0.55$ . Substituting these values in the zero-order equation gives the rate constant $k=5 \times 10^{-4}\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$ . For a zero-order reaction, the half-life is given by $t_{1/2}=\frac{[AB]_{0}}{2k}$ . Putting the values, we get $t_{1/2}=600\text{s}=10\text{min}$ . Therefore, $x=10\text{min}$ (nearest integer).

questions.explanation_text: For a first order reaction $R \rightarrow P$ the integrated rate law is $[R]_{t}=[R]_{0}e^{-k_{1}t}$ where: $[R]_{0}$ = initial concentration of reactant $[R]_{t}$ = concentration after time $t$ Now, the fraction of molecules left undecomposed after time $t$ is $\frac{[R]_{t}}{[R]_{0}}=e^{-k_{1}t}$ So, the fraction of molecules decomposed is $1-\frac{[R]_{t}}{[R]_{0}}=1-e^{-k_{1}t}$ Hence, the correct answer is $1-e^{-k_{1}t}$ So, Option D is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
For a first order reaction

$R \rightarrow P$

the integrated rate law is

$[R]_{t}=[R]_{0}e^{-k_{1}t}$

where:

  • $[R]_{0}$ = initial concentration of reactant

  • $[R]_{t}$ = concentration after time $t$

Now, the fraction of molecules left undecomposed after time $t$ is

$\frac{[R]_{t}}{[R]_{0}}=e^{-k_{1}t}$

So, the fraction of molecules decomposed is

$1-\frac{[R]_{t}}{[R]_{0}}=1-e^{-k_{1}t}$

Hence, the correct answer is

$1-e^{-k_{1}t}$

So, Option D is correct.

questions.explanation_text: Arrhenius equation (NCERT) is $k=Ae^{-E_{a}/RT}$ and in base-10 logarithm form, $logk=logA-\frac{E_{a}}{2.303R}(\frac{1}{T})$ Now check each statement: A. $e^{-E_{a}/RT}$ corresponds to fraction of molecules having kinetic energy less than $E_{a}$ . Incorrect. This factor represents the fraction of molecules having energy equal to or greater than $E_{a}$ (able to cross the energy barrier). B. At a given temperature, lower the $E_{a}$ , faster is the reaction. Correct. From $k=Ae^{-E_{a}/RT}$ , smaller $E_{a} \Rightarrow$ larger $e^{-E_{a}/RT} \Rightarrow$ larger $k$ . C. Increase in temperature by about $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ doubles the rate of reaction. Correct as a common empirical rule mentioned in NCERT: for many reactions, rate approximately doubles for a $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ rise. D. Plot of $logk$ vs $\frac{1}{T}$ gives a straight line with slope $=-\frac{E_{a}}{R}$ . Incorrect. For $log$ (base 10), slope is $-\frac{E_{a}}{2.303R}$ The slope $-\frac{E_{a}}{R}$ is for plotting $lnk$ vs $\frac{1}{T}$ . So, correct statements are B and C only . Correct option: Option C .
questions.explanation_html:
Arrhenius equation (NCERT) is

$k=Ae^{-E_{a}/RT}$

and in base-10 logarithm form,

$logk=logA-\frac{E_{a}}{2.303R}(\frac{1}{T})$

Now check each statement:

A. $e^{-E_{a}/RT}$ corresponds to fraction of molecules having kinetic energy less than $E_{a}$ .

Incorrect. This factor represents the fraction of molecules having energy equal to or greater than $E_{a}$ (able to cross the energy barrier).

B. At a given temperature, lower the $E_{a}$ , faster is the reaction.

Correct. From $k=Ae^{-E_{a}/RT}$ , smaller $E_{a} \Rightarrow$ larger $e^{-E_{a}/RT} \Rightarrow$ larger $k$ .

C. Increase in temperature by about $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ doubles the rate of reaction.

Correct as a common empirical rule mentioned in NCERT: for many reactions, rate approximately doubles for a $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ rise.

D. Plot of $logk$ vs $\frac{1}{T}$ gives a straight line with slope $=-\frac{E_{a}}{R}$ .

Incorrect. For $log$ (base 10), slope is

$-\frac{E_{a}}{2.303R}$

The slope $-\frac{E_{a}}{R}$ is for plotting $lnk$ vs $\frac{1}{T}$ .

So, correct statements are B and C only.

Correct option: Option C.

questions.question_text: For reaction A → P, rate constant $k=1.5 \times 10^{3}s^{-1}$ at $27^{\circ}C$ If activation energy for the above reaction is $60kJmol^{-1}$ , then the temperature (in $^{\circ}C$ ) at which rate constant, $k=4.5 \times 10^{3}s^{-1}$ is ______. (Nearest integer) Given : $log2=0.30$ , $log3=0.48$ , $R=8.3JK^{-1}mol^{-1}$ , $ln10=2.3$
questions.question_html:
For reaction A → P, rate constant $k=1.5 \times 10^{3}s^{-1}$ at $27^{\circ}C$

If activation energy for the above reaction is $60kJmol^{-1}$ , then the temperature (in $^{\circ}C$ ) at which rate constant, $k=4.5 \times 10^{3}s^{-1}$ is ______. (Nearest integer)

Given : $log2=0.30$ , $log3=0.48$ , $R=8.3JK^{-1}mol^{-1}$ , $ln10=2.3$
questions.explanation_text: Use the Arrhenius equation in its two-temperature form: $ln(\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}})=\frac{E_{a}}{R}(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}})$ Given: $k_{1}=1.5 \times 10^{3}s^{-1},T_{1}=27^{\circ}C=300K$ $k_{2}=4.5 \times 10^{3}s^{-1}$ $E_{a}=60kJmol^{-1}=60000Jmol^{-1}$ $R=8.3JK^{-1}mol^{-1}$ First, find the ratio: $\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}=\frac{4.5 \times 10^{3}}{1.5 \times 10^{3}}=3$ So, $ln3=\frac{60000}{8.3}(\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{T_{2}})$ Now convert $ln3$ using the given values: $ln3=2.3log3=2.3 \times 0.48=1.104$ Also, $\frac{60000}{8.3} \approx 7229$ Hence, $1.104=7229(\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{T_{2}})$ Therefore, $\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}=\frac{1.104}{7229}$ $\frac{1.104}{7229} \approx 1.53 \times 10^{-4}$ So, $\frac{1}{T_{2}}=\frac{1}{300}-1.53 \times 10^{-4}$ $\frac{1}{300}=3.33 \times 10^{-3}$ Thus, $\frac{1}{T_{2}}=3.33 \times 10^{-3}-0.153 \times 10^{-3}=3.18 \times 10^{-3}$ $T_{2} \approx \frac{1}{3.18 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 314K$ Now convert into Celsius: $t=314-273=41^{\circ}C$ Hence, the required temperature is $41^{\circ}C$
questions.explanation_html:
Use the Arrhenius equation in its two-temperature form:

$ln(\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}})=\frac{E_{a}}{R}(\frac{1}{T_{1}}-\frac{1}{T_{2}})$

Given:

$k_{1}=1.5 \times 10^{3}s^{-1},T_{1}=27^{\circ}C=300K$

$k_{2}=4.5 \times 10^{3}s^{-1}$

$E_{a}=60kJmol^{-1}=60000Jmol^{-1}$

$R=8.3JK^{-1}mol^{-1}$

First, find the ratio:

$\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}=\frac{4.5 \times 10^{3}}{1.5 \times 10^{3}}=3$

So,

$ln3=\frac{60000}{8.3}(\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{T_{2}})$

Now convert $ln3$ using the given values:

$ln3=2.3log3=2.3 \times 0.48=1.104$

Also,

$\frac{60000}{8.3} \approx 7229$

Hence,

$1.104=7229(\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{T_{2}})$

Therefore,

$\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{T_{2}}=\frac{1.104}{7229}$

$\frac{1.104}{7229} \approx 1.53 \times 10^{-4}$

So,

$\frac{1}{T_{2}}=\frac{1}{300}-1.53 \times 10^{-4}$

$\frac{1}{300}=3.33 \times 10^{-3}$

Thus,

$\frac{1}{T_{2}}=3.33 \times 10^{-3}-0.153 \times 10^{-3}=3.18 \times 10^{-3}$

$T_{2} \approx \frac{1}{3.18 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 314K$

Now convert into Celsius:

$t=314-273=41^{\circ}C$

Hence, the required temperature is

$41^{\circ}C$

Given: $log_{10}k=14.34-\frac{1.5 \times 10^{4}}{T/K}$

From the Arrhenius equation in base-10 form, we write:

$log_{10}k=log_{10}A-\frac{E_{a}}{2.303RT}$

On comparing this with $log_{10}k=14.34-\frac{1.5 \times 10^{4}}{T/K}$ , the coefficient of $\frac{1}{T}$ gives:

$\frac{E_{a_{1}}}{2.303R}=1.5 \times 10^{4}$

Now substitute $R=8.314Jmol^{-1}K^{-1}$ :

$E_{a_{1}}=1.5 \times 10^{4} \times 2.303 \times 8.314$

$E_{a_{1}}=28.7207 \times 10^{4}J$

Convert joules to kilojoules ( $1kJ=10^{3}J$ ):

$E_{a_{1}}=287.207kJ$

Given $E_{a_{2}}=\frac{1}{5}E_{a_{1}}$ , so:

$E_{a_{2}}=\frac{E_{a_{1}}}{5}=\frac{287.207}{5}=57.44kJ$

questions.question_text: Consider a complex reaction taking place in three steps with rate constants $k_{1},k_{2}$ and $k_{3}$ respectively. The overall rate constant $k$ is given by the expression $k=\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}k_{3}}{k_{2}}}$ . If the activation energies of the three steps are 60, 30 and $10kJmol^{-1}$ respectively, then the overall energy of activation in $kJmol^{-1}$ is _________ . (Nearest integer)
questions.question_html: Consider a complex reaction taking place in three steps with rate constants $k_{1},k_{2}$ and $k_{3}$ respectively. The overall rate constant $k$ is given by the expression $k=\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}k_{3}}{k_{2}}}$ . If the activation energies of the three steps are 60, 30 and $10kJmol^{-1}$ respectively, then the overall energy of activation in $kJmol^{-1}$ is _________ . (Nearest integer)
questions.explanation_text: To determine the overall energy of activation for the given complex reaction with rate constants $k_{1}$ , $k_{2}$ , and $k_{3}$ , we start with the expression for the overall rate constant $k$ : $k=\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}k_{3}}{k_{2}}}$ The rate constant can also be expressed in terms of the Arrhenius equation: $A \cdot e^{-E_{a}/RT}=\sqrt{\frac{A_{1}e^{-E_{a_{1}}/RT} \cdot A_{3}e^{-E_{a_{3}}/RT}}{A_{2}e^{-E_{a_{2}}/RT}}}$ By comparing the exponential terms from both sides, we have: $\frac{E_{a}}{RT}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{E_{a_{1}}}{RT}+\frac{E_{a_{3}}}{RT}-\frac{E_{a_{2}}}{RT})$ This simplifies to: $E_{a}=\frac{E_{a_{1}}+E_{a_{3}}-E_{a_{2}}}{2}$ Substituting the given activation energies— $E_{a_{1}}=60\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ , $E_{a_{2}}=30\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ , and $E_{a_{3}}=10\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ : $E_{a}=\frac{60+10-30}{2}=\frac{40}{2}=20\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ Therefore, the overall energy of activation is 20 kJ/mol.
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the overall energy of activation for the given complex reaction with rate constants $k_{1}$ , $k_{2}$ , and $k_{3}$ , we start with the expression for the overall rate constant $k$ :

$k=\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}k_{3}}{k_{2}}}$

The rate constant can also be expressed in terms of the Arrhenius equation:

$A \cdot e^{-E_{a}/RT}=\sqrt{\frac{A_{1}e^{-E_{a_{1}}/RT} \cdot A_{3}e^{-E_{a_{3}}/RT}}{A_{2}e^{-E_{a_{2}}/RT}}}$

By comparing the exponential terms from both sides, we have:

$\frac{E_{a}}{RT}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{E_{a_{1}}}{RT}+\frac{E_{a_{3}}}{RT}-\frac{E_{a_{2}}}{RT})$

This simplifies to:

$E_{a}=\frac{E_{a_{1}}+E_{a_{3}}-E_{a_{2}}}{2}$

Substituting the given activation energies— $E_{a_{1}}=60\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ , $E_{a_{2}}=30\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ , and $E_{a_{3}}=10\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ :

$E_{a}=\frac{60+10-30}{2}=\frac{40}{2}=20\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

Therefore, the overall energy of activation is 20 kJ/mol.

questions.question_text: In a first order decomposition reaction, the time taken for the decomposition of reactant to one fourth and one eighth of its initial concentration are $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ (s), respectively. The ratio $t_{1}/t_{2}$ will be:
questions.question_html: In a first order decomposition reaction, the time taken for the decomposition of reactant to one fourth and one eighth of its initial concentration are $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ (s), respectively. The ratio $t_{1}/t_{2}$ will be:
questions.explanation_text: For a first-order reaction, the integrated rate law is given by: $ln\frac{[A]}{[A]_{0}}=-kt$ where: $[A]_{0}$ is the initial concentration, $[A]$ is the concentration at time $t$ , $k$ is the rate constant. Let's find the times $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ corresponding to when the concentration becomes $\frac{1}{4}[A]_{0}$ and $\frac{1}{8}[A]_{0}$ respectively. For concentration $\frac{1}{4}[A]_{0}$ : Substitute into the integrated rate law: $ln(\frac{1}{4})=-kt_{1}$ Recognizing that $ln(\frac{1}{4})=-ln4$ , we have: $-ln4=-kt_{1}⟹t_{1}=\frac{ln4}{k}$ For concentration $\frac{1}{8}[A]_{0}$ : Substitute into the integrated rate law: $ln(\frac{1}{8})=-kt_{2}$ Recognizing that $ln(\frac{1}{8})=-ln8$ , we have: $-ln8=-kt_{2}⟹t_{2}=\frac{ln8}{k}$ Now, to find the ratio $\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}$ : $\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\frac{\frac{ln4}{k}}{\frac{ln8}{k}}=\frac{ln4}{ln8}$ We can simplify further by expressing the logarithms in terms of $ln2$ : $ln4=ln(2^{2})=2ln2$ $ln8=ln(2^{3})=3ln2$ Thus, $\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\frac{2ln2}{3ln2}=\frac{2}{3}$ So, the ratio $\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}$ is $\frac{2}{3}$ . This corresponds to Option D.
questions.explanation_html:
For a first-order reaction, the integrated rate law is given by:

$ln\frac{[A]}{[A]_{0}}=-kt$

where:

$[A]_{0}$ is the initial concentration,

$[A]$ is the concentration at time $t$ ,

$k$ is the rate constant.

Let's find the times $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ corresponding to when the concentration becomes $\frac{1}{4}[A]_{0}$ and $\frac{1}{8}[A]_{0}$ respectively.

For concentration $\frac{1}{4}[A]_{0}$ :

Substitute into the integrated rate law:

$ln(\frac{1}{4})=-kt_{1}$

Recognizing that $ln(\frac{1}{4})=-ln4$ , we have:

$-ln4=-kt_{1}⟹t_{1}=\frac{ln4}{k}$

For concentration $\frac{1}{8}[A]_{0}$ :

Substitute into the integrated rate law:

$ln(\frac{1}{8})=-kt_{2}$

Recognizing that $ln(\frac{1}{8})=-ln8$ , we have:

$-ln8=-kt_{2}⟹t_{2}=\frac{ln8}{k}$

Now, to find the ratio $\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}$ :

$\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\frac{\frac{ln4}{k}}{\frac{ln8}{k}}=\frac{ln4}{ln8}$

We can simplify further by expressing the logarithms in terms of $ln2$ :

$ln4=ln(2^{2})=2ln2$

$ln8=ln(2^{3})=3ln2$

Thus,

$\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}=\frac{2ln2}{3ln2}=\frac{2}{3}$

So, the ratio $\frac{t_{1}}{t_{2}}$ is $\frac{2}{3}$ .

This corresponds to Option D.

C. At a given temperature, a low activation energy means a fast reaction.

questions.explanation_text: Let’s examine each statement in the light of $k=Ae^{-\frac{E_{a}}{RT}}.$ A. “Arrhenius holds true only for an elementary homogeneous reaction.” • False – it’s an empirical law and is routinely used (and found valid) for complex, composite or even heterogeneous processes. B. “The unit of $A$ is the same as that of $k$ .” • True – since $e^{-E_{a}/RT}$ is dimensionless, $A$ must carry whatever units $k$ has. C. “At a given temperature, a low activation energy means a fast reaction.” • True – smaller $E_{a}$ makes $exp(-E_{a}/RT)$ larger, hence a larger $k$ . D. “ $A$ and $E_{a}$ as used in Arrhenius depend on temperature.” • False – in the simple Arrhenius model both are treated as constants (over modest $T$ -ranges). E. “When $E_{a}≫RT$ , $A$ and $E_{a}$ become interdependent.” • False – although in some data sets you observe a correlation (compensation effect), the basic Arrhenius form still treats them as independent parameters. Therefore the only correct statements are B and C. Answer: B and C only.
questions.explanation_html:
Let’s examine each statement in the light of

$k=Ae^{-\frac{E_{a}}{RT}}.$

A. “Arrhenius holds true only for an elementary homogeneous reaction.”

• False – it’s an empirical law and is routinely used (and found valid) for complex, composite or even heterogeneous processes.

B. “The unit of $A$ is the same as that of $k$ .”

• True – since $e^{-E_{a}/RT}$ is dimensionless, $A$ must carry whatever units $k$ has.

C. “At a given temperature, a low activation energy means a fast reaction.”

• True – smaller $E_{a}$ makes $exp(-E_{a}/RT)$ larger, hence a larger $k$ .

D. “ $A$ and $E_{a}$ as used in Arrhenius depend on temperature.”

• False – in the simple Arrhenius model both are treated as constants (over modest $T$ -ranges).

E. “When $E_{a}≫RT$ , $A$ and $E_{a}$ become interdependent.”

• False – although in some data sets you observe a correlation (compensation effect), the basic Arrhenius form still treats them as independent parameters.

Therefore the only correct statements are B and C.

Answer: B and C only.

However, for radioactive (nuclear) decay processes, the decay constant is essentially independent of external factors such as temperature and pressure. questions.question_html:
For the reaction $A \rightarrow B$ the following graph was obtained. The time required (in seconds) for the concentration of A to reduce to $2.5gL^{-1}$ (if the initial concentration of A was $50gL^{-1}$ ) is . (Nearest integer)

Given : $log2=0.3010$
questions.explanation_text: To determine the time required for the concentration of A to decrease from an initial value of $50gL^{-1}$ to $2.5gL^{-1}$ in the reaction $A \rightarrow B$ , we assume first-order kinetics. Although the graph does not provide a clear indication of the reaction order over the intervals $0-5$ , $5-10$ , and $10-15$ seconds, where the order appears to be zero, we'll proceed with the assumption of first-order kinetics, since the graph is not a straight line. The rate constant $K$ for first-order reactions can be calculated using the formula: $K=\frac{1}{t}ln\frac{A_{0}}{A_{t}}$ For the interval where $A_{0}=40g/L$ and $A_{t}=20g/L$ after 10 seconds: $K=\frac{1}{10}ln\frac{40}{20}$ Now, to find the time $t$ required for the concentration to reduce to $2.5g/L$ : $K=\frac{1}{t}ln\frac{50}{2.5}$ Equating the two expressions for $K$ : $\frac{1}{10}ln2=\frac{1}{t}ln20$ Solving for $t$ : $t=\frac{1.3010 \times 10}{0.3010}=43.3sec$ Therefore, the time required for the concentration to decrease to $2.5g/L$ is approximately 43 seconds.

The rate constant $K$ for first-order reactions can be calculated using the formula:

$K=\frac{1}{t}ln\frac{A_{0}}{A_{t}}$

For the interval where $A_{0}=40g/L$ and $A_{t}=20g/L$ after 10 seconds:

$K=\frac{1}{10}ln\frac{40}{20}$

Now, to find the time $t$ required for the concentration to reduce to $2.5g/L$ :

$K=\frac{1}{t}ln\frac{50}{2.5}$

Equating the two expressions for $K$ :

$\frac{1}{10}ln2=\frac{1}{t}ln20$

Solving for $t$ :

$t=\frac{1.3010 \times 10}{0.3010}=43.3sec$

Therefore, the time required for the concentration to decrease to $2.5g/L$ is approximately 43 seconds.

If the energy barrier with respect to reactant energy for such isomeric transformation is $191.48kJmol^{-1}$ and the frequency factor is $10^{20}$ , the time required for $50%$ molecules of A to become B is __________ picoseconds (nearest integer). $[R=8.314JK^{-1}mol^{-1}]$
questions.question_html:
$A \rightarrow B$

The molecule A changes into its isomeric form B by following a first order kinetics at a temperature of 1000 K . If the energy barrier with respect to reactant energy for such isomeric transformation is $191.48kJmol^{-1}$ and the frequency factor is $10^{20}$ , the time required for $50%$ molecules of A to become B is __________ picoseconds (nearest integer). $[R=8.314JK^{-1}mol^{-1}]$
questions.explanation_text: To determine the time required for 50% of molecule A to change into its isomeric form B, follow these steps: Half-life Formula for First Order Kinetics: The half-life ( $t_{1/2}$ ) for a first-order reaction is given by: $t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{K}$ Calculate the Rate Constant (K): The rate constant $K$ can be calculated using the Arrhenius equation: $K=A \cdot e^{-\frac{E_{a}}{RT}}$ Given: $A$ (frequency factor) = $10^{20}$ $E_{a}$ (activation energy) = $191.48\text{kJ/mol}=191.48 \times 10^{3}\text{J/mol}$ $R$ (universal gas constant) = $8.314\text{J/mol} \cdot \text{K}$ $T=1000\text{K}$ Substitute the values into the Arrhenius equation: $K=10^{20} \times e^{-\frac{191.48 \times 10^{3}}{8.314 \times 1000}}$ Simplify this calculation: $K=10^{20} \times e^{-23.031}$ Simplifying further by recognizing that $e^{-23.031}$ is a very small number, gives: $K \approx \frac{10^{20}}{10^{10}}=10^{10}\text{sec}^{-1}$ Calculate the Half-life: Using the calculated value of $K$ : $t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{10^{10}}=6.93 \times 10^{-11}\text{seconds}$ Convert to Picoseconds: Since $1\text{second}=10^{12}\text{picoseconds}$ : $t_{1/2}=6.93 \times 10^{-11} \times 10^{12}\text{picoseconds}=69.3\text{picoseconds}$ Therefore, the time required for 50% of the molecules of A to become B is approximately 69 picoseconds (nearest integer).
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the time required for 50% of molecule A to change into its isomeric form B, follow these steps:

Half-life Formula for First Order Kinetics:

The half-life ( $t_{1/2}$ ) for a first-order reaction is given by:

$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{K}$

Calculate the Rate Constant (K):

The rate constant $K$ can be calculated using the Arrhenius equation:

$K=A \cdot e^{-\frac{E_{a}}{RT}}$

Given:

$A$ (frequency factor) = $10^{20}$

$E_{a}$ (activation energy) = $191.48\text{kJ/mol}=191.48 \times 10^{3}\text{J/mol}$

$R$ (universal gas constant) = $8.314\text{J/mol} \cdot \text{K}$

$T=1000\text{K}$

Substitute the values into the Arrhenius equation:

$K=10^{20} \times e^{-\frac{191.48 \times 10^{3}}{8.314 \times 1000}}$

Simplify this calculation:

$K=10^{20} \times e^{-23.031}$

Simplifying further by recognizing that $e^{-23.031}$ is a very small number, gives:

$K \approx \frac{10^{20}}{10^{10}}=10^{10}\text{sec}^{-1}$

Calculate the Half-life:

Using the calculated value of $K$ :

$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{10^{10}}=6.93 \times 10^{-11}\text{seconds}$

Convert to Picoseconds:

Since $1\text{second}=10^{12}\text{picoseconds}$ :

$t_{1/2}=6.93 \times 10^{-11} \times 10^{12}\text{picoseconds}=69.3\text{picoseconds}$

Therefore, the time required for 50% of the molecules of A to become B is approximately 69 picoseconds (nearest integer).

questions.question_text: In a reaction $A+B \rightarrow C$ , initial concentrations of $A$ and $B$ are related as $[A]_{0}=8[B]_{0}$ . The half lives of $A$ and $B$ are 10 min and 40 min , respectively. If they start to disappear at the same time, both following first order kinetics, after how much time will the concentration of both the reactants be same?
questions.question_html: In a reaction $A+B \rightarrow C$ , initial concentrations of $A$ and $B$ are related as $[A]_{0}=8[B]_{0}$ . The half lives of $A$ and $B$ are 10 min and 40 min , respectively. If they start to disappear at the same time, both following first order kinetics, after how much time will the concentration of both the reactants be same?
questions.explanation_text: The initial conditions are: $[A]_{0}=8[B]_{0}$ Half-life of A, $[\text{t}_{1/2}]_{A}=10\text{min}$ Half-life of B, $[\text{t}_{1/2}]_{B}=40\text{min}$ Both reactants follow first-order kinetics, and we want to find the time, $t$ , when $[A]_{t}=[B]_{t}$ . Step-by-step Derivation: Write the First-order Rate Equation: For first-order reactions, the concentration $[X]_{t}$ at time $t$ is given by: $[X]_{t}=[X]_{0}e^{-k_{X}t}$ where $k_{X}$ is the rate constant for substance $X$ . Express Half-life through Rate Constant: For first-order reactions, the rate constant $k$ is related to the half-life $\text{t}_{1/2}$ by: $k=\frac{ln2}{\text{t}_{1/2}}$ Substituting the known half-lives: $k_{A}=\frac{ln2}{10}$ $k_{B}=\frac{ln2}{40}$ Set Up the Equality from the Condition $[A]_{t}=[B]_{t}$ : $[A]_{0}e^{-k_{A}t}=[B]_{0}e^{-k_{B}t}$ By inserting the initial condition $[A]_{0}=8[B]_{0}$ , it becomes: $8[B]_{0}e^{-k_{A}t}=[B]_{0}e^{-k_{B}t}$ Simplify and Solve for $t$ : Divide both sides by $[B]_{0}$ : $8e^{-k_{A}t}=e^{-k_{B}t}$ Taking the natural logarithm of both sides: $ln8=-k_{A}t+k_{B}t$ Replace $k_{A}$ and $k_{B}$ with their expressions: $ln8=(\frac{ln2}{10}-\frac{ln2}{40})t$ Simplify Further: $ln8=ln2(\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{40})t$ Simplify $(\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{40})$ to get: $\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{40}=\frac{4-1}{40}=\frac{3}{40}$ So, $ln8=ln2 \times \frac{3}{40} \times t$ Final Expression for $t$ : $t=\frac{ln8}{ln2 \times \frac{3}{40}}$ Calculate the value of $t$ using $ln8=3ln2$ : $t=\frac{3ln2}{ln2 \times \frac{3}{40}}=\frac{40}{1}=40\text{min}$ Therefore, after 40 minutes, the concentration of both reactants A and B will be the same.
questions.explanation_html:
The initial conditions are:

$[A]_{0}=8[B]_{0}$

Half-life of A, $[\text{t}_{1/2}]_{A}=10\text{min}$

Half-life of B, $[\text{t}_{1/2}]_{B}=40\text{min}$

Both reactants follow first-order kinetics, and we want to find the time, $t$ , when $[A]_{t}=[B]_{t}$ .

Step-by-step Derivation:

Write the First-order Rate Equation:

For first-order reactions, the concentration $[X]_{t}$ at time $t$ is given by:

$[X]_{t}=[X]_{0}e^{-k_{X}t}$

where $k_{X}$ is the rate constant for substance $X$ .

Express Half-life through Rate Constant:

For first-order reactions, the rate constant $k$ is related to the half-life $\text{t}_{1/2}$ by:

$k=\frac{ln2}{\text{t}_{1/2}}$

Substituting the known half-lives:

$k_{A}=\frac{ln2}{10}$

$k_{B}=\frac{ln2}{40}$

Set Up the Equality from the Condition $[A]_{t}=[B]_{t}$ :

$[A]_{0}e^{-k_{A}t}=[B]_{0}e^{-k_{B}t}$

By inserting the initial condition $[A]_{0}=8[B]_{0}$ , it becomes:

$8[B]_{0}e^{-k_{A}t}=[B]_{0}e^{-k_{B}t}$

Simplify and Solve for $t$ :

Divide both sides by $[B]_{0}$ :

$8e^{-k_{A}t}=e^{-k_{B}t}$

Taking the natural logarithm of both sides:

$ln8=-k_{A}t+k_{B}t$

Replace $k_{A}$ and $k_{B}$ with their expressions:

$ln8=(\frac{ln2}{10}-\frac{ln2}{40})t$

Simplify Further:

$ln8=ln2(\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{40})t$

Simplify $(\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{40})$ to get:

$\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{40}=\frac{4-1}{40}=\frac{3}{40}$

So,

$ln8=ln2 \times \frac{3}{40} \times t$

Final Expression for $t$ :

$t=\frac{ln8}{ln2 \times \frac{3}{40}}$

Calculate the value of $t$ using $ln8=3ln2$ :

$t=\frac{3ln2}{ln2 \times \frac{3}{40}}=\frac{40}{1}=40\text{min}$

Therefore, after 40 minutes, the concentration of both reactants A and B will be the same.

The half-life ( $t_{1/2}$ ) is calculated as:

$t_{1/2}=\frac{[A]_{0}}{2K}$

Given the slope from the graph is $76.92$ , which equals $\frac{1}{2K}$ . This implies:

$K=\frac{1}{2 \times 76.92}$

Concentration of A at 10 Minutes:

Apply the zero-order kinetics equation:

$[A]_{10}=-Kt+[A]_{0}$

Substituting the values:

$[A]_{10}=-(\frac{1}{2 \times 76.92}) \times 10+2.5=2.435\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Final Concentration:

Convert to scientific notation:

$[A]_{10}=2435 \times 10^{-3}\text{mol L}^{-1}$

Thus, the concentration of A at 10 minutes is approximately $2435 \times 10^{-3}\text{mol L}^{-1}$ .

questions.question_text: Consider the following reaction $A+B \rightarrow C$ The time taken for A to become $1/4^{\text{th}}$ of its initial concentration is twice the time taken to become $1/2$ of the same. Also, when the change of concentration of B is plotted against time, the resulting graph gives a straight line with a negative slope and a positive intercept on the concentration axis. The overall order of the reaction is ________.
questions.question_html:
Consider the following reaction

$A+B \rightarrow C$

The time taken for A to become $1/4^{\text{th}}$ of its initial concentration is twice the time taken to become $1/2$ of the same. Also, when the change of concentration of B is plotted against time, the resulting graph gives a straight line with a negative slope and a positive intercept on the concentration axis.

The overall order of the reaction is ________.
questions.explanation_text: To determine the overall order of the reaction given by $A+B \rightarrow C$ , we can derive the information based on the given details about the kinetics of reactant A and the graphical behavior of reactant B. The first piece of information tells us that the time for the concentration of A to reduce to $1/4$ of its initial concentration ( $[A]_{0}/4$ ) is twice the time it takes to reduce to half of its initial concentration ( $[A]_{0}/2$ ). This characteristic is a hallmark of first-order reactions. In first-order reactions, the time it takes for the concentration of the reactant to reduce to half of its initial value (known as the half-life, $t_{1/2}$ ) is constant and does not depend on the initial concentration. Specifically, the fact that the concentration decreases by a factor of 4 (to $1/4$ its initial value) in twice the time it takes to decrease by a factor of 2 (to $1/2$ its initial value) indicates a constant half-life, consistent with first-order kinetics for reactant A. As for reactant B, the information provided is that a plot of its concentration change over time is a straight line with a negative slope and a positive intercept on the concentration axis. This description matches the behavior of a reactant in a reaction of zero-order kinetics with respect to B, where the rate of reaction is constant and independent of the concentration of B. In zero-order reactions, the concentration of the reactant decreases linearly over time, since the rate of decrease is constant. Therefore, considering the kinetics of both A and B: Reactant A shows first-order kinetics. Reactant B shows zero-order kinetics. The overall order of the reaction is the sum of the individual orders with respect to each reactant, which gives us: $\text{Overall order}=\text{Order with respect to A}+\text{Order with respect to B}=1(A)+0(B)=1.$ Hence, the overall order of the reaction is 1.

questions.question_text: The ratio of $\frac{^{14}C}{^{12}C}$ in a piece of wood is $\frac{1}{8}$ part that of atmosphere. If half life of $^{14}C$ is 5730 years, the age of wood sample is ________ years.
questions.question_html: The ratio of $\frac{^{14}C}{^{12}C}$ in a piece of wood is $\frac{1}{8}$ part that of atmosphere. If half life of $^{14}C$ is 5730 years, the age of wood sample is ________ years.
questions.explanation_text: The given problem involves calculating the age of a wood sample using the carbon-14 dating method. Carbon-14 ( $^{14}C$ ) is a radioactive isotope of carbon that decays over time, and its ratio compared to carbon-12 ( $^{12}C$ ) can be used to date organic materials. The ratio of $\frac{^{14}C}{^{12}C}$ in the wood is $\frac{1}{8}$ th of that in the atmosphere, suggesting the $^{14}C$ has decayed. The half-life of $^{14}C$ is given as 5730 years, which is the time for half the $^{14}C$ to decay. To solve for the age of the wood, we use the formula for radioactive decay: $N=N_{0}e^{-\lambda t},$ where $N$ is the remaining amount of $^{14}C$ , $N_{0}$ is the original amount of $^{14}C$ , $\lambda$ is the decay constant, and $t$ is the time (age of the wood). Since the ratio $\frac{N}{N_{0}}=\frac{1}{8}$ , we infer that $N=\frac{N_{0}}{8}$ . Substituting into the decay equation and solving for $t$ , first we find the decay constant $\lambda$ : $\lambda=\frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}=\frac{0.693}{5730}.$ Substitute $\lambda$ and rearrange to solve for $t$ : $t=\frac{ln(8)}{\lambda}=\frac{ln(8)}{0.693} \times 5730=3 \times 5730=17190\text{years}.$ This calculation shows that the wood sample is 17190 years old.

The ratio of $\frac{^{14}C}{^{12}C}$ in the wood is $\frac{1}{8}$ th of that in the atmosphere, suggesting the $^{14}C$ has decayed. The half-life of $^{14}C$ is given as 5730 years, which is the time for half the $^{14}C$ to decay.

To solve for the age of the wood, we use the formula for radioactive decay:

$N=N_{0}e^{-\lambda t},$

where $N$ is the remaining amount of $^{14}C$ , $N_{0}$ is the original amount of $^{14}C$ , $\lambda$ is the decay constant, and $t$ is the time (age of the wood).

Since the ratio $\frac{N}{N_{0}}=\frac{1}{8}$ , we infer that $N=\frac{N_{0}}{8}$ . Substituting into the decay equation and solving for $t$ , first we find the decay constant $\lambda$ :

$\lambda=\frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}=\frac{0.693}{5730}.$

Substitute $\lambda$ and rearrange to solve for $t$ :

$t=\frac{ln(8)}{\lambda}=\frac{ln(8)}{0.693} \times 5730=3 \times 5730=17190\text{years}.$

This calculation shows that the wood sample is 17190 years old.

questions.question_text: For a reaction taking place in three steps at same temperature, overall rate constant $K=\frac{K_{1}K_{2}}{K_{3}}$ . If $Ea_{1},Ea_{2}$ and $Ea_{3}$ are 40, 50 and $60kJ/mol$ respectively, the overall $Ea$ is ________ $kJ/mol$ .
questions.question_html: For a reaction taking place in three steps at same temperature, overall rate constant $K=\frac{K_{1}K_{2}}{K_{3}}$ . If $Ea_{1},Ea_{2}$ and $Ea_{3}$ are 40, 50 and $60kJ/mol$ respectively, the overall $Ea$ is ________ $kJ/mol$ .
questions.explanation_html:
$\begin{aligned} & K=\frac{K_{1} \cdot K_{2}}{K_{3}}=\frac{A_{1} \cdot A_{2}}{A_{3}} \cdot e^{-\frac{(E_{a_{1}}+E_{a_{2}}-E_{a_{3}})}{RT}} \\ & A \cdot e^{-E_{a}/RT}=\frac{A_{1}A_{2}}{A_{3}} \cdot e^{-\frac{(E_{a_{1}}+E_{a_{2}}-E_{a_{3}})}{RT}} \end{aligned}$

$E_{a}=E_{a_{1}}+E_{a_{2}}-E_{a_{3}}=40+50-60=30kJ/mole.$

questions.question_html: For a reaction $A\overset{K_{1}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}B\overset{K_{2}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}C$ If the rate of formation of B is set to be zero then the concentration of B is given by :

Therefore, we have: $K_{1}[A]=K_{2}[B]$ Solving for $[B]$ , we get: $[B]=\frac{K_{1}}{K_{2}}[A]$ Therefore, the correct concentration of $B$ is: Option D: $(\frac{K_{1}}{K_{2}})[A]$

questions.question_text: Consider the following first order gas phase reaction at constant temperature $A(g) \rightarrow 2B(g)+C(g)$ If the total pressure of the gases is found to be 200 torr after 23 $sec$ . and 300 torr upon the complete decomposition of A after a very long time, then the rate constant of the given reaction is ________ $\times 10^{-2}s^{-1}$ (nearest integer) [Given : $log_{10}(2)=0.301$ ]
questions.question_html:
Consider the following first order gas phase reaction at constant temperature $A(g) \rightarrow 2B(g)+C(g)$

If the total pressure of the gases is found to be 200 torr after 23 $sec$ . and 300 torr upon the complete decomposition of A after a very long time, then the rate constant of the given reaction is ________ $\times 10^{-2}s^{-1}$ (nearest integer)

[Given : $log_{10}(2)=0.301$ ]
questions.explanation_text: To find the rate constant of the first-order reaction indicated, let us first understand the reaction dynamics based on the total pressure change over time. The reaction is: $A(g) \rightarrow 2B(g)+C(g)$ Initially, only A is present. As the reaction progresses, A decreases, and B and C are formed. For each mole of A that reacts, a total of 3 moles of gas are produced (2 moles of B and 1 mole of C), leading to an increase in the total pressure of the system if the volume remains constant. At the start: Total pressure due to A only. Finally, when A has completely decomposed: Total pressure is due to 3 times the initial amount of A, as no A is left and for every mole of A decomposed, 3 moles of gas (2B + 1C) are produced. The total pressure change thus directly relates to the extent of reaction, i.e., how much A has decomposed into B and C. The total pressure at 23 sec is 200 torr, and the final total pressure is 300 torr after a very long time, indicating that the pressure increases by 100 torr due to the complete decomposition of A. To use this information, we need to understand the relationship between pressure change and concentration in a closed system, especially for a first-order reaction. For a first-order reaction: $ln(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]})=kt$ Where: $[A]_{0}$ is the initial concentration (or in this context, partial pressure), $[A]$ is the concentration (or partial pressure) at time t, $k$ is the rate constant, and $t$ is the time. Let's denote the initial total pressure due to A as $P_{0}$ . At complete decomposition, the pressure increase is from the conversion of A to 2B + C which increases the total pressure to 300 torr, indicating that initially, $P_{0}$ must have been 100 torr since the pressure increase is due to the tripling effect of the reaction, completing to 300 torr. At 23 sec, the total pressure is at 200 torr. This means 100 torr is due to the unreacted A, and the additional 100 torr is from the formation of 2B + C. Given the nature of the reaction (1:3 stoichiometry of A to the total gas), we can deduce that at 23 seconds, half of A has reacted because the pressure due to the products matches the pressure due to the unreacted A. Hence, at 23 sec, $[A]=\frac{1}{2}[A]_{0}$ . Plugging this into the first-order reaction formula: $ln(\frac{[A]_{0}}{\frac{1}{2}[A]_{0}})=kt$ $ln(2)=k \times 23$ Given that $log_{10}(2)=0.301$ , and knowing that $ln(2)=log_{e}(2)$ (where $log_{e}(2) \approx 0.693$ , for conversion from base 10 to e we can use the natural logarithm of 2 directly), we have: $0.693=k \times 23$ $k=\frac{0.693}{23}=0.0301s^{-1}$ When expressed in the format requested, $k=3.01 \times 10^{-2}s^{-1}$ . Rounding to the nearest integer, $k=3 \times 10^{-2}s^{-1}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To find the rate constant of the first-order reaction indicated, let us first understand the reaction dynamics based on the total pressure change over time. The reaction is:

$A(g) \rightarrow 2B(g)+C(g)$

Initially, only A is present. As the reaction progresses, A decreases, and B and C are formed. For each mole of A that reacts, a total of 3 moles of gas are produced (2 moles of B and 1 mole of C), leading to an increase in the total pressure of the system if the volume remains constant.

At the start: Total pressure due to A only.

Finally, when A has completely decomposed: Total pressure is due to 3 times the initial amount of A, as no A is left and for every mole of A decomposed, 3 moles of gas (2B + 1C) are produced.

The total pressure change thus directly relates to the extent of reaction, i.e., how much A has decomposed into B and C.

The total pressure at 23 sec is 200 torr, and the final total pressure is 300 torr after a very long time, indicating that the pressure increases by 100 torr due to the complete decomposition of A.

To use this information, we need to understand the relationship between pressure change and concentration in a closed system, especially for a first-order reaction. For a first-order reaction:

$ln(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]})=kt$

Where: $[A]_{0}$ is the initial concentration (or in this context, partial pressure), $[A]$ is the concentration (or partial pressure) at time t, $k$ is the rate constant, and $t$ is the time.

Let's denote the initial total pressure due to A as $P_{0}$ . At complete decomposition, the pressure increase is from the conversion of A to 2B + C which increases the total pressure to 300 torr, indicating that initially, $P_{0}$ must have been 100 torr since the pressure increase is due to the tripling effect of the reaction, completing to 300 torr.

At 23 sec, the total pressure is at 200 torr. This means 100 torr is due to the unreacted A, and the additional 100 torr is from the formation of 2B + C. Given the nature of the reaction (1:3 stoichiometry of A to the total gas), we can deduce that at 23 seconds, half of A has reacted because the pressure due to the products matches the pressure due to the unreacted A.

Hence, at 23 sec, $[A]=\frac{1}{2}[A]_{0}$ . Plugging this into the first-order reaction formula:

$ln(\frac{[A]_{0}}{\frac{1}{2}[A]_{0}})=kt$

$ln(2)=k \times 23$

Given that $log_{10}(2)=0.301$ , and knowing that $ln(2)=log_{e}(2)$ (where $log_{e}(2) \approx 0.693$ , for conversion from base 10 to e we can use the natural logarithm of 2 directly), we have:

$0.693=k \times 23$

$k=\frac{0.693}{23}=0.0301s^{-1}$

When expressed in the format requested, $k=3.01 \times 10^{-2}s^{-1}$ . Rounding to the nearest integer, $k=3 \times 10^{-2}s^{-1}$ .

questions.question_text: Time required for $99.9%$ completion of a first order reaction is _________ times the time required for completion of $90%$ reaction.(nearest integer)
questions.question_html: Time required for $99.9%$ completion of a first order reaction is _________ times the time required for completion of $90%$ reaction.(nearest integer)
questions.explanation_text: To determine the time required for a certain level of completion ( $x%$ ) of a first-order reaction, we can use the formula that relates the time $t$ , the rate constant $k$ , and the concentration of the reactant. The formula for a first-order reaction, when expressed in terms of the initial concentration $[A]_{0}$ and the concentration at time $t$ , $[A]_{t}$ , is given by the integrated rate law for first-order reactions: $ln(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{t}})=kt$ For a given percentage of completion, we use the fact that $[A]_{t}=[A]_{0}(1-\frac{x}{100})$ , where $x$ is the percentage completion. Thus, the equation becomes: $ln(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{0}(1-\frac{x}{100})})=kt$ Simplifying, we get: $ln(\frac{1}{1-\frac{x}{100}})=kt$ Let's calculate the time required for $99.9%$ and $90%$ : For $99.9%$ completion ( $x=99.9%$ ): $ln(\frac{1}{1-\frac{99.9}{100}})=kt_{99.9}$ $ln(\frac{1}{0.001})=kt_{99.9}$ $ln(1000)=kt_{99.9}$ For $90%$ completion ( $x=90%$ ): $ln(\frac{1}{1-\frac{90}{100}})=kt_{90}$ $ln(\frac{1}{0.1})=kt_{90}$ $ln(10)=kt_{90}$ Since $k$ is a constant for a given reaction at a constant temperature, we can compare the times $t_{99.9}$ and $t_{90}$ directly by comparing the logarithmic values: $\frac{t_{99.9}}{t_{90}}=\frac{ln(1000)}{ln(10)}$ Using the property of logarithms, we know that $ln(1000)=3ln(10)$ because $1000=10^{3}$ , so: $\frac{t_{99.9}}{t_{90}}=\frac{3ln(10)}{ln(10)}=3$ Therefore, the time required for $99.9%$ completion of a first-order reaction is $3$ times the time required for completion of $90%$ of the reaction. The nearest integer to this value is $3$ .
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the time required for a certain level of completion ( $x%$ ) of a first-order reaction, we can use the formula that relates the time $t$ , the rate constant $k$ , and the concentration of the reactant. The formula for a first-order reaction, when expressed in terms of the initial concentration $[A]_{0}$ and the concentration at time $t$ , $[A]_{t}$ , is given by the integrated rate law for first-order reactions:

$ln(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{t}})=kt$

For a given percentage of completion, we use the fact that $[A]_{t}=[A]_{0}(1-\frac{x}{100})$ , where $x$ is the percentage completion. Thus, the equation becomes:

$ln(\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]_{0}(1-\frac{x}{100})})=kt$

Simplifying, we get:

$ln(\frac{1}{1-\frac{x}{100}})=kt$

Let's calculate the time required for $99.9%$ and $90%$ :

  • For $99.9%$ completion ( $x=99.9%$ ):

$ln(\frac{1}{1-\frac{99.9}{100}})=kt_{99.9}$

$ln(\frac{1}{0.001})=kt_{99.9}$

$ln(1000)=kt_{99.9}$

  • For $90%$ completion ( $x=90%$ ):

$ln(\frac{1}{1-\frac{90}{100}})=kt_{90}$

$ln(\frac{1}{0.1})=kt_{90}$

$ln(10)=kt_{90}$

Since $k$ is a constant for a given reaction at a constant temperature, we can compare the times $t_{99.9}$ and $t_{90}$ directly by comparing the logarithmic values:

$\frac{t_{99.9}}{t_{90}}=\frac{ln(1000)}{ln(10)}$

Using the property of logarithms, we know that $ln(1000)=3ln(10)$ because $1000=10^{3}$ , so:

$\frac{t_{99.9}}{t_{90}}=\frac{3ln(10)}{ln(10)}=3$

Therefore, the time required for $99.9%$ completion of a first-order reaction is $3$ times the time required for completion of $90%$ of the reaction. The nearest integer to this value is $3$ .

questions.question_text: $NO_{2}$ required for a reaction is produced by decomposition of $N_{2}O_{5}$ in $CCl_{4}$ as by equation $2N_{2}O_{5(g)} \rightarrow 4NO_{2(g)}+O_{2(g)}$ The initial concentration of $N_{2}O_{5}$ is $3molL^{-1}$ and it is $2.75molL^{-1}$ after 30 minutes. The rate of formation of $NO_{2}$ is $x \times 10^{-3}molL^{-1}min^{-1}$ , value of $x$ is _________. (nearest integer)
questions.question_html:
$NO_{2}$ required for a reaction is produced by decomposition of $N_{2}O_{5}$ in $CCl_{4}$ as by equation

$2N_{2}O_{5(g)} \rightarrow 4NO_{2(g)}+O_{2(g)}$

The initial concentration of $N_{2}O_{5}$ is $3molL^{-1}$ and it is $2.75molL^{-1}$ after 30 minutes.

The rate of formation of $NO_{2}$ is $x \times 10^{-3}molL^{-1}min^{-1}$ , value of $x$ is _________. (nearest integer)
questions.explanation_text: Rate of reaction (ROR) $\begin{aligned} & =-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta[N_{2}O_{5}]}{\Delta t}=\frac{1}{4}\frac{[NO_{2}]}{\Delta t}=\frac{\Delta[O_{2}]}{\Delta t} \\ & ROR=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta[N_{2}O_{5}]}{\Delta t}=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(2.75-3)}{30}molL^{-1}min^{-1} \\ & ROR=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(-0.25)}{30}molL^{-1}min^{-1} \\ & \text{ROR}=\frac{1}{240}molL^{-1}min^{-1} \end{aligned}$ Rate of formation of $NO_{2}=\frac{\Delta[NO_{2}]}{\Delta t}=4 \times ROR$ $=\frac{4}{240}=16.66 \times 10^{-3}molL^{-1}min^{-1}≃17 \times 10^{-3}\text{.}$
questions.explanation_html:
Rate of reaction (ROR)

$\begin{aligned} & =-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta[N_{2}O_{5}]}{\Delta t}=\frac{1}{4}\frac{[NO_{2}]}{\Delta t}=\frac{\Delta[O_{2}]}{\Delta t} \\ & ROR=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta[N_{2}O_{5}]}{\Delta t}=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(2.75-3)}{30}molL^{-1}min^{-1} \\ & ROR=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(-0.25)}{30}molL^{-1}min^{-1} \\ & \text{ROR}=\frac{1}{240}molL^{-1}min^{-1} \end{aligned}$

Rate of formation of $NO_{2}=\frac{\Delta[NO_{2}]}{\Delta t}=4 \times ROR$

$=\frac{4}{240}=16.66 \times 10^{-3}molL^{-1}min^{-1}≃17 \times 10^{-3}\text{.}$
